q: Which Azure Machine Learning tool helps a data scientist assess a model's errors and fairness across different groups of people?
exp: The Responsible AI dashboard in Azure Machine Learning brings together tools such as error analysis and fairness assessment, so you can see where a model performs worse for certain groups. Azure Advisor gives general recommendations, Cost Management tracks spending, and Azure Policy enforces resource rules; none of them evaluate model fairness.

q: For each of the following statements about fairness, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Fairness means that an AI system gives everyone the same result, whatever their situation.
A fairness check before the first release is enough, even if the model is updated later.
How the training data was collected does not affect fairness.
exp: No for the first: fairness means similar outcomes for people in similar situations; different situations can justify different outcomes. No for the second: a new model version or new data can introduce new disparities, so fairness checks should be repeated. No for the third: unrepresentative or biased data is a common cause of unfair models.

q: Which statement describes the reliability and safety principle?
opts: AI systems should be as cheap as possible for each customer
AI systems should work safely in unexpected conditions
AI systems should run only at night
AI systems should never be updated after they are released
exp: Reliability and safety means an AI system should behave as intended, resist harmful manipulation and respond safely to situations it was not designed for. Cost, time of day and avoiding updates are not responsible AI principles, and updates are often needed to keep a system reliable.

q: Complete the sentences by selecting the correct option for each blank.
tpl: Testing a model with inputs that it did not see during training helps check {0}. Planning what to do when the system fails in production means preparing {1}.
exp: Testing with unseen and unusual inputs shows whether the system behaves reliably and safely outside its training data. An incident response plan defines how to detect, contain and fix failures in production. Transparency and inclusiveness are other principles, and pricing or marketing plans do not handle failures.

q: A team wants to fine-tune a model on support emails that contain customer names and phone numbers. Which step best supports privacy?
opts: Publish the emails so others can check the data
Remove or mask the personal data before training
exp: Removing or masking personal data before training means the model cannot learn and later repeat customers' names and phone numbers, which protects privacy. Publishing the emails exposes the data, and training longer or using a bigger model changes quality and cost but not privacy.

q: Which TWO are privacy considerations when you design a generative AI chat app? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
opts: Use the largest available context window
Tell users how their data is used and stored
Pick the model with the most parameters
Avoid putting unnecessary personal data into prompts
exp: Being clear about how user data is used and stored, and sending only the personal data a task needs, both protect privacy. Context window size and parameter count affect capability and cost, and a color theme is a design choice; none of them protect personal data.

q: A benefits app uses plain language, short steps and a simple layout so that people with cognitive disabilities can use it. Which principle does this support?
exp: Designing for people with different abilities, including cognitive disabilities, is inclusiveness. Fairness is about equal outcomes for similar people, accountability is about who answers for the system, and privacy and security is about protecting data.

q: Match each group of users to an inclusive design feature that helps them. Each feature can be used once or not at all.
targets: Screen reader support and image alt text
exp: Screen readers and alt text help blind users, captions and transcripts help deaf users, voice input helps people who cannot type easily, and multilingual support helps people who speak other languages. Temperature changes how varied model output is and does nothing for accessibility.

ctx: A bank's website chat gives information about loans. Many customers later say they did not realize they were talking to an AI system and thought the answers were personal advice from an employee.
q: Which responsible AI principle should the bank address first?
exp: Customers should know when they are interacting with AI and understand what it can and cannot do, which is transparency. Clearly disclosing the chat as AI and explaining its limits would fix the misunderstanding. Nothing in the scenario points to unequal outcomes, accessibility barriers or unsafe behavior.

q: Which THREE actions support the transparency principle? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
opts: Hide the model's errors from users
Label content that was generated by AI
Tell users that they are talking to an AI system
Explain the system's limitations to users
Remove the notice that the app uses AI
exp: Labeling generated content, explaining limitations and saying that users are talking to AI all help people understand what they are dealing with. Hiding errors and removing the notice take that understanding away.

q: Who should approve the release of a high-impact AI system in an organization that follows the accountability principle?
opts: A designated owner or review board
Any user who asks for it and has an account
Nobody, because AI systems govern themselves
exp: Accountability requires clear human ownership and governance, such as named owners or a review board that applies the organization's AI policy before release. A model cannot be accountable, random users are not responsible for the system, and AI systems do not govern themselves.

q: For each of the following statements about accountability, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Accountability means that someone must be able to audit how an AI system was used.
Using a model from an outside vendor removes your organization's accountability for how it is used.
When a person reviews high-risk AI decisions, the organization no longer needs records of them.
exp: Yes for the first: audit records show what the system did and support investigation. No for the second: the organization that deploys an AI system remains accountable for its use, even when the model comes from a vendor. No for the third: human oversight and records work together, because records let people check later what was decided and why.

q: Users report that a company's AI assistant is giving harmful advice. Put the incident response steps in the correct order. Not every step is used.
items: Investigate the cause and fix it
Ignore the reports until the next planned release
Detect and confirm the problem through monitoring and user reports
Inform affected users and record the lessons learned
Contain the problem, for example by turning off the feature or tightening filters
exp: A responsible response first confirms the problem, then contains it quickly to stop further harm, then finds and fixes the root cause, and finally communicates with affected people and records lessons to prevent repeats. Ignoring reports conflicts with accountability and reliability and safety.

q: What does pre-training mean for a model such as GPT?
opts: Writing the system message for the first version
Choosing the Azure region where the model will run
The first training on a large, general dataset
Setting the quota and the region of a new deployment
exp: Pre-training is the initial training on a very large and broad dataset, during which the model learns general language patterns; 'pre-trained' is the P in GPT. Writing a system message, choosing a region and setting quota happen later, when you use or deploy the model.

q: Why can many large language models answer questions in several languages?
opts: They were trained on text written in many languages
They call a translation service for every request
They use a separate deployment for each language
They cannot; they only work in English
exp: Large language models learn from training data that includes many languages, so they can understand and write in those languages directly. They do not route every request through a translation service or need a deployment per language, although quality can vary between languages.

q: For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Fine-tuning adds documents to the prompt and leaves the model's weights unchanged.
Grounding data must be added to the prompt again when the next request needs it.
Grounding can permanently change the model's weights.
exp: No for the first: that describes grounding; fine-tuning is further training that updates the model's weights. Yes for the second: grounding, such as RAG, adds relevant content to each prompt at request time, and the model does not remember it afterward. No for the third: grounding affects only the current request; the model itself is not changed.

q: Match each description to the term it describes. Each term can be used once or not at all.
items: Learning general patterns from a huge dataset
Adapting a model with your own labeled examples
Using a trained model to generate a response to a prompt
Adding retrieved documents to the prompt
exp: Pre-training learns general patterns from a huge dataset, fine-tuning adapts the model with your examples, inference is using the trained model to produce output, and retrieval augmented generation adds retrieved documents to prompts. Quota allocation is a deployment setting, not a stage of how models learn or answer.

q: Complete the sentences by selecting the correct option for each blank.
tpl: Given the text 'The capital of France is', a language model predicts the most likely next {0}. The size of a model is often described by its number of {1}.
exp: Language models generate text by predicting the next token, here most likely 'Paris'. Model size is usually given as the number of parameters, the learned weights inside the network. Images, regions and deployments are not what the model predicts or how its size is measured.

q: A company wants a language model that it can download and run on its own servers when needed. Which kind of model fits?
opts: A model that is available only as a hosted API
An open-weight model, such as a Phi model
exp: Open-weight models, such as Microsoft's Phi family, publish their weights, so they can be deployed in Foundry or run on your own infrastructure. Models offered only as hosted APIs cannot be downloaded, and image-generation APIs and speech services are different kinds of services.

q: Your app must send a 300-page document to a model in a single request. Which model property matters most?
exp: The context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can process in one request, so a very long document needs a model with a large context window, or you must split the document. Price, image generation and speech output do not decide whether the document fits.

q: Which TWO pieces of information on a model card help you decide whether a model fits your solution? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opts: The color of the provider's logo
The supported input and output types
The context window and maximum output length
The day of the week it was released
exp: Supported inputs and outputs tell you whether the model can handle your data, such as images or audio, and the context window and output limits tell you how much it can process and return. Logo colors, authors' home towns and release weekdays say nothing about fitness for a task.

q: For each of the following statements about choosing a model, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Reasoning models usually take longer to answer than small chat models.
Every model in the catalog supports every language equally well.
A smaller model can be good enough for simple classification tasks.
exp: Yes for the first: reasoning models spend extra time and tokens thinking before they answer. No for the second: language support and quality differ between models, so you should check the model card and test. Yes for the third: simple tasks often do not need the largest model, and smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

q: You want a model to bring up new topics in a brainstorming session instead of staying on the same ideas. Which parameter should you increase?
exp: Presence penalty lowers the chance of tokens that have already appeared at all, which pushes the model toward new topics. Max tokens limits length, a stop sequence ends output at a marker, and seed is used to make outputs more repeatable rather than more varied.

q: During testing you want the same prompt and settings to give more repeatable outputs between runs. Which parameter helps?
exp: The seed parameter asks the service to sample in a repeatable way, so identical requests with the same seed and settings tend to return the same output; determinism is best effort, not guaranteed. Presence penalty changes topic variety, a stop sequence ends output, and max tokens limits length.

q: Match each parameter to its effect. Each effect can be used once or not at all.
targets: Limits how long the response can be
Controls how random the choice of each token is
Ends the output when a given string appears
Reduces repetition of the same tokens
Sets the data zone of the deployment
exp: Temperature controls randomness, max tokens limits length, a stop sequence ends output at a chosen string, and frequency penalty reduces repetition. The data zone is decided by the deployment type, such as Data Zone Standard, not by a request parameter.

q: Complete the sentences about deployment types.
tpl: Pay-per-token billing with processing in any Azure region is offered by {0}. Reserved capacity billed in provisioned throughput units is offered by {1}.
exp: Global Standard charges per token and routes requests across Azure's global capacity. Provisioned deployments reserve throughput measured in provisioned throughput units, which you pay for whether or not you use it. Global Batch is for asynchronous bulk jobs, and Data Zone Standard is pay-per-token within a data zone.

q: What happens when a standard deployment receives more requests than its tokens-per-minute quota allows?
opts: Billing stops until the next minute begins
The deployment is deleted and must be created again
exp: When traffic exceeds the deployment's rate limits, the service throttles extra requests and returns 429 errors, so clients should retry with backoff or you should raise the quota. Exceeding quota does not change accuracy, stop billing or delete the deployment.
